title: Episode 174: Franklin D. Roosevelt: The First Hundred Days and the Fireside Chats (1921–1934)
description:
On March 4, 1933, when Franklin Delano Roosevelt took the oath of office as the thirty-second President of the United States, the American republic was on the brink of total collapse. Every bank in thirty-eight states was shuttered, industrial production had fallen by half, and fifteen million Americans were jobless. Yet twelve years earlier, Roosevelt had fought and survived his own personal apocalypse: struck down by polio at age thirty-nine at his summer cottage on Campobello Island, he was left permanently paralyzed from the waist down. Transforming his personal agony into boundless political empathy, Roosevelt delivered an inaugural address that electrified the world: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' In an astonishing whirlwind of one hundred days, Roosevelt declared a national Bank Holiday, spoke directly into millions of living rooms in his first Fireside Chat, and enacted an unprecedented legislative avalanche that forged the modern New Deal. Discover the resurrection of American hope.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we begin our epic journey into the life and presidency of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. In the darkest hour of the Great Depression, when democracy itself seemed to be crumbling across the globe, an aristocrat in leg braces summoned the courage of a shattered nation. Here is George with the story of the ordeal at Campobello, the miracle of the First Hundred Days, and the voice that restored America's soul.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ARISTOCRAT OF HYDE PARK
Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born in January 1882 on a majestic estate overlooking the Hudson River in Hyde Park, New York. The only child of a wealthy, patrician lineage that traced back to seventeenth-century Dutch New Amsterdam, young Franklin grew up in an atmosphere of aristocratic privilege, private tutors, European tours, and doting maternal affection from his formidable mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt. Educated at elite Groton School and Harvard University, Franklin was deeply inspired by the heroic political career of his fifth cousin, President Theodore Roosevelt. In 1905, on St. Patrick's Day, Franklin married Theodore's favorite niece, Eleanor Roosevelt, with the sitting President himself walking the shy, brilliant bride down the aisle. Possessing dashing good looks, a radiant smile, and infectious optimism, Franklin followed TR's exact footsteps into public service: winning a New York State Senate seat at age twenty-eight, serving as Woodrow Wilson's dynamic Assistant Secretary of the Navy during World War I, and running as the Democratic vice presidential nominee in 1920. Though the ticket went down in defeat, thirty-eight-year-old Roosevelt had established himself as the undisputed golden boy and Roosevelt possessed a natural gift for human connection, an instinctive ease among everyday working people, and an aura of effortless nobility that drew people irresistibly into his orbit.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CRUCIBLE OF CAMPOBELLO
In August 1921, the golden boy's world was shattered into a thousand pieces. While vacationing with Eleanor and his children at their summer cottage on Campobello Island off the coast of New Brunswick, Canada, thirty-nine-year-old Roosevelt spent an exhausting day fighting a forest fire and swimming in the frigid waters of the Bay of Fundy. That evening, he collapsed with severe chills, paralyzing headaches, and excruciating muscle pain. Within seventy-two hours, the paralysis crept inexorably upward through his legs, leaving him completely unable to stand, walk, or support his own weight from the waist down. He had contracted acute poliomyelitis—polio. His domineering mother pleaded with him to retire permanently to Hyde Park as an invalid country squire, but Eleanor and his devoted political advisor, Louis Howe, adamantly urged him to fight. For seven agonizing years, Roosevelt engaged in brutal, daily physical rehabilitation. Discovering the buoyant, mineral-rich thermal waters of Warm Springs, Georgia, he swam for hours, laughing through the pain and purchasing the resort to create a worldwide rehabilitation center for fellow polio victims. Though he would never walk unassisted again, requiring heavy seven-pound steel braces locked at the knee and the iron grip of a son's arm, the crucible of suffering fundamentally transformed Roosevelt. The arrogant young aristocrat was purged away, replaced by an extraordinary depth of patience, boundless empathy for human suffering, and an unshakeable, Polio stripped away Franklin Roosevelt's physical vanity and arrogance, replacing them with a profound spiritual strength and a deep personal understanding of vulnerability that resonated with millions who were suffering.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RETURN AND THE 1932 CAMPAIGN
In 1928, Roosevelt made a sensational political return, narrowly winning election as Governor of New York while his close ally Al Smith was defeated in the presidential race. When the Great Depression struck a year later, Governor Roosevelt acted with bold, innovative speed, creating the Temporary Emergency Relief Administration to distribute millions in food, clothing, and cash to destitute New Yorkers. By 1932, with the national economy in complete ruins, Roosevelt was the commanding contender for the Democratic presidential nomination. Flying through turbulent storms to Chicago to accept the nomination in person—a dramatic break with the stuffy tradition of waiting for a formal notification committee—Roosevelt strode to the rostrum on his steel braces and electrified the convention hall. 'I pledge you, I pledge myself,' he thundered, 'to a new deal for the American people.' In the autumn campaign, accompanied by Eleanor's tireless investigative travels, Roosevelt radiated vibrant health and cheerful confidence, promising bold, persistent experimentation. On election day, November 8, 1932, the American people delivered a monumental verdict, giving Roosevelt twenty-three million votes to Hoover's fifteen million and His victory was not merely a rejection of Herbert Hoover, but an overwhelming mandate from a desperate electorate for bold national leadership and immediate action.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 'NOTHING TO FEAR BUT FEAR ITSELF'
During the agonizing four-month transition between November 1932 and March 1933, the American economic system came to a complete, catastrophic standstill. Panic-stricken depositors besieged thousands of banks, draining gold and currency reserves. On the morning of Inauguration Day, March 4, 1933, the Governors of New York and Illinois signed emergency proclamations shuttering the financial exchanges; by noon, every single bank in thirty-eight states was closed, and trading was halted nationwide. Under a leaden gray sky on the East Portico of the Capitol, Franklin D. Roosevelt gripped the lectern, pushed his steel braces tight, and faced a crowd of one hundred thousand anxious, silent citizens. His voice rang out over the radio microphones with clarion power and magnificent calm: 'This is preeminently the time to speak the truth, the whole truth, frankly and boldly... So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.' He declared that the money changers had fled the temple of our civilization, and promised that if normal constitutional procedures failed to solve the crisis, he would ask Congress for broad executive power to wage a war against the emergency, as great as the power that would be given to him if we The ringing delivery transformed the mood of the capital; where there had been gloom and paralysis, Roosevelt injected immediate courage, purpose, and unmistakable authority.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BANK HOLIDAY AND THE FIRST FIRESIDE CHAT
Roosevelt wasted not a single hour. On March 6, his second day in office, he invoked the wartime Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 to declare a mandatory nationwide 'Bank Holiday,' temporarily closing every financial institution in the United States to halt the lethal drain on reserves. Summoning a special session of Congress for March 9, Roosevelt submitted the Emergency Banking Act. In an astonishing demonstration of national unity, the House of Representatives passed the bill by unanimous voice vote in just thirty-eight minutes—using a single rolled-up newspaper draft because printed copies were not yet off the press—and the Senate confirmed it hours later. But the real triumph occurred on Sunday evening, March 12, 1933. Sitting in front of radio microphones in the basement Diplomatic Reception Room of the White House, Roosevelt delivered his very first 'Fireside Chat.' Speaking with soothing intimacy and everyday clarity, he addressed sixty million listeners: 'My friends, I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking... I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress.' The effect was an instantaneous psychological miracle. On Monday morning, March 13, when the sound banks reopened, long lines formed around the country—not to withdraw money, but to deposit hundreds of millions of dollars back into the vaults. Through the magic of radio and sincere human communication, Roosevelt accomplished in eight days what four years of financial maneuvers had failed to achieve: he restored fundamental faith in American institutions.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WHIRLWIND OF THE FIRST HUNDRED DAYS
Having saved the banking system, Roosevelt unleashed the most astonishing legislative deluge in American history—the legendary 'First Hundred Days.' Surrounded by his 'Brain Trust' of brilliant academic advisors and Cabinet officers like Labor Secretary Frances Perkins—the first woman ever appointed to a presidential cabinet—Roosevelt submitted bill after revolutionary bill to a stunned and receptive Congress. In rapid succession, Congress passed the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), sending two hundred and fifty thousand unemployed young men to plant trees, combat soil erosion, and build state parks across America. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) provided subsidies to rescue desperate farmers from foreclosure. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) brought dams, flood control, and cheap hydroelectric power to seven impoverished southern states. The Glass-Steagall Banking Act permanently separated commercial and investment banking and created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to guarantee ordinary savings accounts forever. The Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA) distributed direct cash to millions of starving families, while the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA) established industrial fair-practice codes under the famous Blue Eagle emblem. In one hundred breathless days, the entire relationship between the American citizen and their The New Deal established the enduring principle that the federal government possesses an affirmative constitutional duty to protect its citizens from economic catastrophe and guarantee basic security.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VOICE OF HOPE AND THE NEW AMERICAN DAWN
By the time Congress adjourned on June 16, 1933, the psychological atmosphere of the United States had been utterly transformed. The sense of hopeless doom and paralyzing defeat that had hung over the nation for four bitter years had vanished, replaced by an exhilarating spirit of dynamic experimentation and shared civic purpose. Millions of ordinary working-class families hung framed photographs of Franklin D. Roosevelt on their living room walls beside portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Jesus Christ. Thousands of letters poured into the White House mailroom every single day—scrawled on scrap paper by coal miners in Pennsylvania, sharecroppers in Mississippi, and factory workers in Detroit—pouring out their hearts to a president they felt personally understood their struggles. Fierce critics accused him of socialism, dictatorship, and reckless spending, but Roosevelt smiled warmly through his cigarette holder, welcoming their hatred and reaffirming his faith in democratic capitalism. The paralyzed aristocrat from Hyde Park had looked fear in the eye, stood tall on his steel braces, and In doing so, Roosevelt proved that democracy was not an obsolete relic incapable of meeting modern crises, but a resilient, living framework capable of renewing itself through hope, courage, and bold action.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Franklin D. Roosevelt's First Hundred Days resurrected American hope and laid the permanent foundations of the modern social contract. But the Great Depression was far from conquered, and dark clouds of global fascism were beginning to gather across the horizon in Europe and Asia. Next week, we continue our Roosevelt series with his dramatic reelection in 1936, the controversial Supreme Court packing battle, the creation of Social Security, and America's transformation into the great 'Arsenal of Democracy' as the world plunged into World War II. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
